source.title_on_document: Group-AI collaboration enhances creativity performance: The roles of perspective-taking and AI utilization strategies

supplement.where: The text refers to 'Supplementary Figure 2A' (p. 12) and 'Supplementary Figure 2B' (p. 15). No URL or appendix is named, and the PDF has no supplement section. Main-text Figure 2 (p. 13) shows the same two classification schemes and may be what these references mean.
supplement.holds: The classification schemes for perspective-taking behaviors (2A) and AI prompt strategies (2B). No creativity statistic is said to sit in a supplement: arm means, SDs, and mixed-model coefficients with SEs are in the main text (pp. 15-16), and the mediation total effects are in Figure 5 (p. 21).

paper_design_summary: In a laboratory study in China, 96 university students were analyzed after 100 were recruited and four were excluded for failing to follow task instructions (p. 7, Section 2.1; pp. 26-27, Section 4). Participants were randomly paired, and each person completed a scientific divergent application task in group-AI, individual-AI, and human-only group conditions, with condition order counterbalanced and labeled 'Random Presentation' in Figure 1B (pp. 7-9, Section 2.2). ChatGPT-4o and DeepSeek rated idea usefulness and originality, and fluency and high-quality idea fluency counted the outputs; mixed-effects models used a Subject ID random effect, but the aggregation of pair-condition creativity scores is not stated (p. 10, Section 2.3; pp. 15-16, Section 3.1).

studies.label: Within-subject lab experiment: group-AI vs individual-AI vs human-only group (scientific divergent application task)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Participants were randomly paired into two-person teams. Each pair then completed all three conditions (group-AI, individual-AI, human-only group), with the order of conditions and the task items counterbalanced across participants. The text says each team was 'randomly assigned to one of the three' conditions, and Figure 1B labels the order 'Random Presentation'. The randomization procedure is not described.
assignment.quote: Subsequently, each team was randomly assigned to one of the three collaborative innovation conditions
assignment.locator: p. 7, Section 2.1 ('within-subjects experimental design'); pp. 7-8, Section 2.2 Procedure; p. 9, Figure 1B ('Random Presentation')
assignment.prereg_locator: No preregistration is mentioned. p. 7 reports an a priori power analysis (G*Power 3.1, f = 0.25, minimum of 56 participants).

arms.name: Group-AI (G-AI)
arms.description: Two-person team takes turns posting one idea per turn in a shared (public) chat panel in QQ Chat. Each member has their own ChatGPT-4o and may ask it one task-related question during each of their own turns. 15 minutes.

arms.name: Individual-AI (I-AI)
arms.description: Each participant works one-on-one with ChatGPT-4o. The idea panel is private, so participants see only their own input. 15 minutes.

arms.name: Human-only group (G)
arms.description: Two-person team takes turns posting ideas in a shared (public) chat panel. The AI interface is disabled. 15 minutes. The human partner is the other aid; no generative AI was available.

participants.exclusions: 100 participants were recruited and four were excluded for failing to follow task instructions; 96 people were analyzed (p. 7, Section 2.1). The described procedure places random pairing before standardized instructions, the pre-task questionnaire, condition assignment, and task performance (pp. 7-8, Section 2.2), consistent with task-instruction exclusions occurring after pairing. The paper does not print a count at pairing or assignment, specify exactly when exclusions were applied, or explain what happened to excluded participants' partners. Counts at assignment remain null. Every analyzed participant completed all three conditions (p. 8); arm n_analyzed values count these same people, not independent creativity scores or regression observations.
participants.who: University students (abstract: '96 university students'); 64 women; mean age 21.91 (SD 3.51); paid 60 RMB.
participants.quote: Four participants were excluded for failing to follow task instructions, resulting in a final sample of 96
participants.locator: p. 7, Section 2.1 Participants; p. 1, Abstract ('96 university students'); pp. 26-27, Section 4 ('participants in this study were recruited from China')

ai_tool.how_used: Participants typed prompts to ChatGPT-4o in a panel beside the idea panel (Figure 1A). In group-AI, each member had their own ChatGPT-4o and could ask it a single task-related question during each of their own turns. In individual-AI, participants worked one-on-one with ChatGPT-4o. Participants either copied an AI idea verbatim or adapted it. The authors collected 209 task-related prompts in group-AI (after removing two unrelated prompts, p. 14) and 313 in individual-AI (p. 15).

task.description: Scientific divergent application task (SDAT), adapted from the 10-item instrument of Wan et al. (2025): each item introduces a novel material and asks for novel applications of it. Three items were randomly selected (transparent ceramics, electronic skin, crystal resin), and each condition used a different item, with item assignment counterbalanced. In the pair conditions, partners took turns posting one idea per turn in a QQ chat window.
task.duration: 15 minutes per condition, after a 5-minute pre-test questionnaire (Figure 1B, p. 9)

outcomes.name: Creative usefulness
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Extent to which the ideas could be realistically applied, 5-point scale (1 = not at all useful, 5 = very useful), rated by two LLMs (ChatGPT-4o and DeepSeek); ICC between the two models 0.74 (p. 10). Mixed-effects model with Subject ID as random effect and condition as fixed effect (p. 15); random-effect variance 0.09 (SE = 0.09) (p. 15). The four control variables (ideational behavior, group preference, algorithm aversion, AI trust) are said to enter 'the subsequent analyses' (p. 10), but Section 3.1 does not say whether they enter these models. PROCESS Model 4 mediation models print total effects in Figure 5 (p. 21) and direct and indirect effects in Section 3.4 (p. 20). Direct effects are net of a post-treatment mediator and are not contrast results (for example, G-AI vs G net of direct human perspective taking: b = 0.77, p < 0.001, 95% CI [0.63, 0.91], p. 20). The analysis unit is unconfirmed: Section 3.1 specifies a Subject ID random effect but does not report the aggregation of ideas in the two pair conditions or the number of observations behind the condition means (pp. 10, 15-16). unit and n_units are therefore null. The arm counts describe analyzed people and cannot be used as independent outcome counts. The Figure 5 totals come from separate PROCESS Model 4 analyses with a condition dummy (pp. 19-20, Section 3.4), not from the Section 3.1 mixed-effects models. The human perspective-taking mediator is summed across both partners (p. 11); the process tests report F(1, 47) and t(142) (pp. 17-18). These details suggest team aggregation in pair conditions, but neither the outcome rows nor the mediation sample sizes are stated. Do not assume the same unit or dependence adjustment for the two model types.

eligibility.reason: All three criteria are met for the saved preprint. Criterion 1: every participant completed all three conditions; the text describes random team assignment and counterbalanced condition order, and Figure 1B labels condition presentation 'Random Presentation' (pp. 7-9, Section 2.2 and Figure 1B). ChatGPT-4o was available in two conditions and disabled in the human-only condition (pp. 8-9). Criterion 2: 96 people were analyzed after four exclusions from 100 recruits, and the same participants completed all conditions (pp. 7-8); these people are counted once, irrespective of whether scores were aggregated by team. Criterion 3: usefulness and originality were scored on the ideas by ChatGPT-4o and DeepSeek, and fluency and high-quality fluency counted the produced ideas (p. 10, Section 2.3). Unreported aggregation and model sample sizes prevent confirmation of the precision basis, not eligibility. The exact randomization algorithm and exclusion handling are also unreported. This assessment applies to the preprint on file; the journal version has not been checked.

one_line_finding: Pairs in which each member had ChatGPT-4o produced ideas that two LLM judges rated more useful than human-only pairs (M = 4.09 vs 3.24; β = 0.84, SE = 0.04) and than people working alone with ChatGPT-4o (3.34; β = 0.74, SE = 0.06), and more original (3.68 vs 2.74 and 2.70; β = 0.94, SE = 0.05 and β = 0.98, SE = 0.07), while fluency did not differ and working alone with AI did not differ from human-only pairs (p > 0.05) (pp. 15-16, Section 3.1; p. 17, Figure 3).
open_questions: The creativity-score aggregation and analysis rows remain unknown: Section 3.1 specifies Subject ID random effects, whereas human perspective-taking is summed across both partners and process tests report F(1, 47) and t(142) (pp. 10-11, 15-18). The paper does not state whether pair-condition outcome scores were assigned to individuals, pooled by team, or repeated across partners, nor the sample sizes and dependence adjustments used for Figure 5. This also covers reconciliation.agreed_fields_checked's unconfirmed participant-unit item. Data and analysis code with participant and team identifiers would settle it; the people-count and output-scoring criteria already hold.

The exact method used to randomize condition order is not described. Counterbalancing in Section 2.2 and 'Random Presentation' in Figure 1B support criterion 1 (pp. 7-9); authors could supply the assignment algorithm and sequence allocation.

The procedure places pairing before task instructions, consistent with the exclusions occurring after pairing, but does not specify the exact exclusion stage, counts at assignment, or treatment of excluded participants' partners (pp. 7-8, Sections 2.1-2.2). Authors could supply participant and partner flow; the final analyzed count is established.

Whether the control variables named on p. 10 entered the Section 3.1 mixed-effects models, and why their coefficients differ from the separate Figure 5 total effects (pp. 15-16, 19-21). Data and model code would distinguish adjustment, aggregation, and sample differences.

Whether 'Supplementary Figure 2A' and '2B' (pp. 12, 15) refer to main-text Figure 2 (image p. 13; caption p. 14) or separate supplementary material. The named material concerns coding schemes; no creativity statistic is described as available only there.

The Journal of Computer Assisted Learning version (10.1002/jcal.70223) has not been compared with the saved preprint. The journal version would settle post-review changes to methods, statistics, and the internal numerical inconsistencies recorded in notes; eligibility is supported by the saved preprint.
notes: The source is the blinded EdArXiv preprint identified in retrieval.json; the journal version has not been checked. No author name appears in the PDF despite the p. 1 note. Creativity judges are ChatGPT-4o and DeepSeek, so the rated outcomes are automated_score. Human-only group is other_aid under the current form spec because the partner is the aid. Group-AI vs human-only group remains ai_vs_bau because both use the same pair setup; individual-AI vs human-only group is ai_vs_active; group-AI vs individual-AI is ai_design, with differences in human partnership and the one-question-per-turn rule in addition to the shared AI tool. All four creativity outcomes are paper-primary (p. 15); no overall creativity rating is reported. Outcome unit and n_units are null because pair-condition aggregation and observation counts are not stated. Removed arm_means_sds_ns flags because printed means and SDs lack confirmed outcome-level ns; those means and SDs remain in reported. The Figure 5 totals and SEs were verified visually against the PDF and are retained as separate PROCESS results, with their analysis units unresolved. No derived effect size or reconstructed analysis-unit count has been entered. Pooling precision requires confirmation of the independent units and dependence adjustment. Process measures omitted from the creativity outcome list include perspective-taking counts and adoption rates, AI-use frequency and strategy counts, and response time (pp. 17-23). No across-people diversity estimate or separately analyzed after-AI outcome is reported. Internal source discrepancies are preserved: AI-use frequency is M = 4.53, p = 0.003, d = 0.59 in Section 3.3 (p. 19), versus M = 4.35, p = 0.01, d = 0.51 in Section 3.5 (p. 22), with t(142) = 3.02 in both. Figure 5C (p. 21) prints a direct effect of 7.21 (SE 1.04), while Section 3.4 (p. 20) prints 7.01. Figure 5F marks the direct effect 2.68 with two stars, while p. 20 says p < 0.001. The Figure 5 caption (p. 22) calls the mediator HQAPAR, while panels E and F use HQAPTR; Figures 5 and 6 captions use CN while the panels use CO. The Discussion's claim that individual-AI increased idea volume is on p. 23, while Section 3.1 (p. 16) reports no fluency difference. Ethics approval HR2-0252-2024 and SPSS 26 with PROCESS are reported on pp. 7 and 15. The reconciliation object is retained unchanged as history; the final resolutions supersede its participant-unit assumption, human-only arm code, and p. 22 Discussion locator.

open_items.item: Creativity-score aggregation, model observation counts, and dependence adjustment, including the unconfirmed participant-unit item in reconciliation.agreed_fields_checked. Affects precision, not the three eligibility criteria.
Exact condition-order randomization method. Criterion 1 is already supported by the assignment text and Figure 1B; authors could supply sequence allocation.
Precise exclusion stage, counts at assignment, and handling of excluded participants' partners. The 96 analyzed people already establish criterion 2.
Covariates in the mixed-effects models and the source of differences from the separate PROCESS total effects. Model code and data would resolve this extraction issue.
Whether Supplementary Figure 2A/2B are separate material or references to main-text Figure 2. The references concern coding schemes, not missing eligibility evidence or outcome statistics.
Post-review changes and internal numerical discrepancies in the saved preprint. The journal version would permit comparison; all three eligibility criteria are supported by the saved preprint.
